Where it began

Sanjay Bangar was born in Beed, Maharashtra, on 11 October 1972, and went to school at Saint Francis De Sales High School. He came up through the youth sides of Maharashtra and Mumbai, but it was with Railways that he made his name, as a medium-pace bowler with a sound, patient defence.

Railways reached the Ranji Trophy final in 2000–01 and lost to Baroda. A season later they beat Baroda to take the title, and Bangar's part in it earned him a place in India's squad to face England.

The player

He needed only two Tests to reach three figures: batting at number seven against Zimbabwe at Nagpur, he finished on 100 not out. In England in 2002 he was moved up to open at Headingley and, in conditions that swung and seamed, made a patient 68 alongside Rahul Dravid on the first day. Later in the match he chipped in with two wickets, and India won by an innings, a rare thing away from home in those days.

In 12 Tests between 2001 and 2002 he made 470 runs at 29.38, with a hundred and three fifties, and took 7 wickets with a best of 2 for 23. He was also part of the squad that reached the World Cup final in 2003.

What made him special

He was the kind of cricketer captains love: he would bat wherever he was needed and bowl whenever he was asked. For Railways he was a giant. As captain he led them to the Ranji Trophy and the Irani Trophy in 2004–05 and to the one-day national title a season later. He joined Vijay Hazare as only the second man with the Ranji Trophy double of 6,000 runs and 200 wickets.

His bowling was steady rather than frightening, and Test batters seldom lost sleep over it. He made up for that by being so hard to dislodge with the bat.

Away from the middle

After 20 years of playing he retired in January 2013 and turned to coaching, where he was greatly valued. He took Kings XI Punjab to the IPL final in 2014, and from that year until 2019 he worked with the India team, mostly as batting coach. Several leading batters, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma among them, credited him with helping their batting grow. He went on to coach Royal Challengers Bangalore, became head of cricket development at Punjab Kings and became a familiar voice as a commentator. He also wrote a piece for a 2012 book about Rahul Dravid.

And finally

Along the way he took a Bachelor of Commerce degree and the intermediate course for company secretaries. It was a sensible back-up plan, and cricket never gave him the chance to use it.
